1. Purpose and Scope
This document establishes the official enterprise engineering guidelines for writing, testing, packaging, and maintaining
Python applications across Apex Global Technologies. All backend microservices, data pipelines, automation scripts, and
machine learning components must comply with these standards.
2. Python Runtime and Virtual Environment Management
To avoid global package pollution, dependency collisions, and environment drift across development and production
environments, all Python projects must execute within an isolated virtual environment (venv).
2.1 Creating and Activating a Virtual Environment
Apex projects standardize on the standard library venv module. Follow this canonical procedure when setting up any
Python repository:
# Step 1: Navigate to project root directory
cd ~/projects/enterprise-backend
# Step 2: Create a virtual environment named .venv using the standard Python 3 interpreter
python3 -m venv .venv
# Step 3: Activate the virtual environment
# On POSIX systems (Linux / macOS):
source .venv/bin/activate
# On Windows (PowerShell):
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
# On Windows (Command Prompt):
.\.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
# Step 4: Verify the active interpreter points to the local virtual environment
which python   # Expected output: .../enterprise-backend/.venv/bin/python
python --version   # Must output Python 3.11.x or 3.12.x
Deactivation Command
To exit the isolated virtual environment at any time, execute the shell command: deactivate . 
2.2 Dependency Pinning and Package Management
All production dependencies must be strictly locked with cryptographic hashes using pip-tools or pinned

python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
# Install production dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt
# Install development and testing dependencies
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
3. Code Style, Linting, and Formatting Standards
Apex enforces strict code uniformity across all repositories. Automated CI checks will reject pull requests that fail
formatting gates:
PEP 8 Compliance: Strict adherence to Python Enhancement Proposal 8 (Style Guide for Python Code).
Ruff Formatter & Linter: Apex uses ruff as our ultra-fast universal Python linter and formatter. Maximum line
length is locked at 88 characters (consistent with Black conventions).
Import Sorting: Standardize imports using isort rules built into Ruff: standard library first, third-party packages
second, internal local modules third, each separated by a blank line.
Type Annotations (PEP 484 / PEP 526): All function signatures, method parameters, and return types must include
explicit type annotations. Repositories enforce mypy --strict in CI pipelines.
# Example of compliant enterprise Python code with strict typing
from typing import Optional, List
from dataclasses import dataclass
import logging
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class KnowledgeChunk:
    chunk_id: str
    document_id: str
    text_content: str
    embedding_score: float
def retrieve_top_chunks(query_vector: List[float], top_k: int = 5) -> List[KnowledgeChunk]:
    if not query_vector:
        logger.warning("Empty query vector supplied to retrieve_top_chunks.")
        return []
    # Vector retrieval execution logic
    return []
4. Testing, Quality Assurance, and Logging
Pytest Framework: All automated tests must be authored using pytest . Test files must follow the naming pattern 
test_*.py located in a top-level tests/ directory.
Coverage Floor: Pull requests must maintain a minimum of 85% line and branch test coverage verified via pytest
--cov=src --cov-fail-under=85 .
Structured JSON Logging: Raw print() statements are forbidden in production code. Applications must
configure Python's standard logging module to emit structured JSON logs with correlation IDs ( request_id ).
